title: Internal Insurance Portal
description: I owned a large-scale internal portal end to end, consolidating fragmented frontends into one Nx monorepo and migrating a monolith into a micro-frontend architecture.

seo.title: Internal Insurance Portal — Case Study
seo.description: How I consolidated fragmented frontends into a single Nx monorepo and cut the JS bundle by roughly 45% for a hospital-facing insurance portal.

items.src: Hospital-side staff relied on this portal for agent-assisted discharge and claims processing, but the frontend that powered it was split across multiple codebases with no shared source of truth. The same component existed in slightly different forms in each repo, and a fix in one place rarely made it to the others.

src: Duplicated components drifted out of sync across codebases.
The monolithic app's bundle size slowed load times on hospital-floor devices.
Releases required coordinating changes across every fragmented repo at once.

items.src: I unified the fragmented frontends into a single Nx-powered monorepo first, so there was one place to fix a bug once. With that foundation in place, I migrated the monolithic application into a micro-frontend architecture, splitting it along the actual workflow boundaries: discharge, claims, and agent tooling.

src.title: Consolidate before splitting
src.desc: Merging into one monorepo first meant the later micro-frontend split happened against a single, consistent codebase instead of four diverging ones.

src.title: Code splitting and lazy loading as defaults
src.desc: Every new micro-frontend shipped with code splitting, lazy loading, and tree shaking on by default, not as an afterthought, so bundle discipline held as the app grew.

items.src: Cutting bundle size without breaking workflows

The monolith's bundle had grown large enough to slow load times on the older hardware used hospital-side. I profiled the bundle, then applied code splitting, lazy loading, and tree shaking across the newly split micro-frontends to bring it down without touching the discharge and claims logic staff depended on daily.
Coordinating across backend, DevOps, QA, and product

Owning the portal end to end meant the frontend architecture decisions had to work for every team downstream. I ran the frontend as its own workstream with a clear API contract, so backend, DevOps, and QA could move without waiting on frontend release cycles.

src.label: Reduction in duplicate code after the Nx consolidation
Micro-frontends shipping on independent release cycles

items.src: It's tempting to split a struggling monolith straight into micro-frontends. I learned it's worth unifying the codebase first: a single, consistent source of truth makes every decision after it, from module boundaries to bundle budgets, easier to get right.
